idiom_name: protocol algebra with an associatedtype witness, passed explicitly (type-erased when stored)
implementation_notes: Swift has no higher-kinded types, so the algebra becomes a protocol whose associated type plays the role of the interpreted type: `protocol ExprSym { associatedtype Repr; func lit(_ i: Int) -> Repr; func add(_ l: Repr, _ r: Repr) -> Repr }`, interpreters are types conforming to it (`typealias Repr = Int` for the evaluator, `String` for the printer), and the program is a generic function `<S: ExprSym>(_ s: S) -> S.Repr`, so the protocol witness is threaded explicitly. What replaces the classic structure: protocol witnesses and generic constraints instead of implicit type-class resolution; because an existential cannot name the associated type, storing or passing the interpreter as a value requires a hand-written type-erasure wrapper (a closure box) - that is the manual part. Justified for testable interpreters in a Swift package; for a single interpretation, direct types are simpler.
pitfalls: An existential `any ExprSym` cannot expose `Repr`, so an interpreter that must be stored in a property or an array needs a type-erasing wrapper that boxes each operation - budget for that boilerplate.

Every generic instantiation produces a specialised copy of the program: many interpreters mean code bloat, and `@inlinable`/opaque return types can hide the witness so tests cannot substitute an interpreter.
Protocols cannot be resolved implicitly, so the witness is threaded by hand; a defaulted parameter hides that and silently pins the production interpreter into the program.
Value-type interpreters are copied on capture - a mutating or class-based interpreter that records calls must be a reference type, or recordings vanish with the copy.
